entry.title: Sticky Routing That Never Expires Isn't Sticky It's Permanent
entry.summary: Session affinity is a simple idea: route a client to the same backend node it used The failure mode isn't in the assignment logic. It's in what happens after the A routing layer assigns each client to a specific backend instance and persists This is correct, as far as it goes. The problem is what "least-loaded" is measured Nothing ever deleted a row. Not on client disconnect, not on any timer, not on any Each individual row is completely correct the client it points to really was And it degrades anyway. A node that happens to pick up more assignments early Given enough time and enough churn, you get a small number of nodes stuck This is the part worth sitting with: the failure has no direct symptom pointing What you actually observe is imbalance, or unexplained Generalize this past routing tables specifically: any system that writes state on absence of a corresponding event has this Add a TTL to the assignment, refreshed on every successful use. An active client's The choice of TTL over an explicit delete-on-disconnect is deliberate, not every reason a client goes silent, because it doesn't depend on being One more detail worth knowing if you're building this on DynamoDB specifically: native TTL is best-effort, not instantaneous. AWS documents it as typically gone by the time you next If the same client also has some local state on the node an idle timeout that If a piece of state gets written on one event and there's no code path that removes absence of a future event, that's worth a second look not because it's obviously wrong, but because it's the specific shape of bug that produces no error, passes every individual-write test, and shows up later as something that looks completely unrelated.

entry.title: One Key for Every PBX: The Issabel Framework Hardcoded JWT Flaw (CVE-2026-89026)
entry.summary:
One Key for Every PBX: The Issabel Framework Hardcoded JWT Flaw (CVE-2026-89026)
Issabel Framework, an open-source unified communications platform built around Asterisk, shipped with a single HS256 signing key hardcoded in its pbxapi component. Because every deployment used the same value, an attacker who learned it could mint a valid bearer token for any installation. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-89026, carries a CVSS base score of 9.8, and was fixed in commit b97dbaf. The pbxapi layer validates JSON Web Tokens signed with that shared secret. With the key known, an attacker generates a token the service accepts and calls the management originate function. That interface passes a System parameter through to Asterisk, which executes the supplied string with the privileges of t…
